problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} & \frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{2}{5} & \frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ given above. Which of the following statements are true?

- ${A}^{T}=A$
- ${A}^{2}=A$
- $A$ is an orthogonal projection matrix

activity_context.topic_title: Projection Matrices, Linear Transformations and Their Properties

examples.problem:
Which of the following are orthogonal projection matrices?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071876/assets/5b3093e1c65624c862d949706ed5922ab8078beac752d4e7347c71be993580d8.png)
examples.worked_solution:
Recall that $Q$ is an orthogonal projection matrix if and only if $Q^2=Q$ and $Q^T=Q.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- $A$ is *not* an orthogonal projection matrix. We have
$A^T = A$
but 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =A\cdot A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 \\ 5 & 10\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne A.\end{aligned}
$$

- $B$ is *not* an orthogonal projection matrix. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}^{T}\ne B.\end{aligned}
$$

- $C$ is an orthogonal projection matrix. Indeed,
$C^T = C$
and

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{2} & =C\cdot C \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} & \frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{2}{5} & \frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} & \frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{2}{5} & \frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}20 & 10 \\ 10 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} & \frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{2}{5} & \frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}] \\  & =C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$C$ only."

feedback.problem:
Find a matrix that defines the orthogonal projection of ${R}^{3}$ onto the plane whose parametric equation is $r=sv+tw$, where

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the matrix ${P}_{S}=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}$ maps any vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ onto its orthogonal projection in the subspace $S$ spanned by the columns of the matrix $A.$ 

Notice that the plane $r=sv+tw$ is actually the subspace $\text{Span}{v,w}.$ 
Hence, we have 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S} & =A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]{([\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
